claims.text: House-made wheat noodles are boiled to order in shared ramen water; no gluten-free preparation exists, so cross-contamination with wheat is unavoidable.
The broth's defining element is a special soy-sauce (shoyu) tare made with traditional Kyoto soy sauce; Japanese soy sauce is normally brewed with wheat, so the broth contains wheat-derived gluten.

Broth is built on shellfish dashi (oyster, clam, shrimp) and the shop's centerpiece is pork chashu; no vegan or vegetarian bowl is offered, so there is no animal-free option to protect from cross-contact.
The broth is finished with a soy-based (shoyu) seasoning and soy sauce is available at the table for adjustment — standard wheat-containing shoyu, not gluten-free.

The defining feature of the bowl is a deep, jet-black soy-sauce broth/tare in the Shinpuku Saikan style; soy-sauce tare of this type is standard wheat-based shoyu, so the ramen should be treated as containing wheat.
Broth is a pork-bone and chicken base with pork-loin chashu, and the yakimeshi is cooked with pork; there are no plant-based items, so cross-contact with animal products is total.
The bowls are shoyu-tonkotsu based; the soy-sauce tare used in this style of ramen standardly contains wheat.
The broths are finished with soy-sauce-based tare (Japanese soy sauce / white soy sauce), which is wheat-containing, and the noodles are wheat ramen noodles.

name: 麺家 しょうりん (Menya Shourin)

claims.text: Standard ramen tare and an emulsified chicken-pork broth are used; no allergen breakdown is published, but a wheat-based shoyu tare is typical for this style.
All bowls are animal-based (chicken-pork bone broth, meat toppings, chicken paste); no vegan or vegetarian preparation exists, so cross-contact is unavoidable for plant-based diners.
A tantanmen specialist serving wheat noodles in sesame/soy-seasoned animal broth alongside shrimp wonton; gluten is central to the menu and no gluten-free handling has been described.
Soy sauce is provided as a table condiment and the seasoning base is sesame/soy-style; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, and no wheat-free tamari is indicated.
The broth is animal-based (chicken with some pork) and shrimp wonton is on the menu, so the kitchen is not set up for vegan separation.
The signature abura-soba is dressed in a house-made sweet-spicy soy (shoyu) tare, which is wheat-based; combined with the wheat noodles this dish is not gluten-free.
